title: Sweet Wine
description: Four ways to keep sugar in a wine, and why the best sweet wines are never cloying.
L: How a wine ends up sweet
Explain the two routes to a sweet wine
Explain why acidity matters in sweet wine

A wine is sweet when sugar remains after fermentation. There are two routes. Stop fermentation before the yeast has eaten all the sugar, by chilling, filtering or adding spirit. Or concentrate the sugar in the grapes so much that yeast can't finish, stopping naturally at around 11 to 14% alcohol with plenty of sugar left.
Stop the yeast, or overload it with sugar

Grapes can be concentrated in four main ways: by noble rot, a fungus that dries the berries; by late harvesting, leaving grapes on the vine; by freezing them on the vine, for ice wine; or by drying them after picking. Each removes water, so sugar, acid and flavour all become more intense.
Noble rot, late harvest, freezing, drying
Which methods concentrate sugar in the grape before fermentation?
Adding spirit stops fermentation; it doesn't concentrate the grape. That's how fortified wines like Port keep their sugar.

Sugar without acidity tastes cloying, like syrup. The great sweet wines have high acidity to balance it: Riesling, Chenin Blanc, Furmint and Sémillon blended with Sauvignon are typical. That's why a Mosel Auslese or a Tokaji can feel fresh despite 100 g/l of sugar or more.
Why do the best sweet wines not taste cloying?
They have high acidity to balance the sugar
They have no sugar at all
High acidity cuts through sugar, keeping the wine fresh and lively.
Sweet wines either stop fermentation early or start with concentrated grapes
Noble rot, late harvest, freezing and drying concentrate sugar
High acidity keeps sweet wines from tasting cloying
A fungus that makes great wine
Name the great noble rot wines

Noble rot is the fungus Botrytis cinerea. On ripe, healthy grapes in the right conditions, it pierces the skin, letting water evaporate. Berries shrivel, sugar and acidity concentrate, and new flavours appear: honey, marmalade, apricot and ginger. The same fungus in wet weather becomes grey rot, which ruins the crop.
Botrytis: noble when dry, grey when wet

Noble rot needs humid, misty mornings, often from rivers or lakes, to let the spores grow, followed by warm, dry afternoons that stop it turning into grey rot. Infection is uneven, so pickers pass through the vineyard several times, choosing only shrivelled berries. Yields can be tiny, sometimes a glass per vine.
Mist then sun; picking in several passes
Which conditions favour noble rot rather than grey rot?
Misty mornings and dry, sunny afternoons
Morning humidity lets the fungus grow; dry afternoons stop it becoming destructive grey rot.

Sauternes and Barsac, in Bordeaux, use Sémillon and Sauvignon Blanc, near the cool Ciron river. Tokaji Aszú, in Hungary, uses Furmint. In Germany and Austria, Beerenauslese and Trockenbeerenauslese are made from botrytised berries. The Loire's Coteaux du Layon and Quarts de Chaume use Chenin Blanc.
Sauternes, Tokaji, TBA, Coteaux du Layon
Match each wine to its main grape.
Each of these is made from noble rot grapes, with a high-acid grape at its heart.
Noble rot is Botrytis cinerea concentrating ripe grapes
It needs misty mornings and dry afternoons
Sauternes, Tokaji Aszú and TBA are its great wines
Explain how late harvest wines are made
Explain how ice wine is made
Name the main regions for each

Leave grapes on the vine past normal ripeness and they keep gaining sugar, then start to shrivel, losing water. This is late harvest. Labels show it as Vendanges Tardives in Alsace, Spätlese and Auslese in Germany, or simply Late Harvest elsewhere. Some late harvest wines also have a share of noble rot.
Late harvest: longer on the vine

Ice wine, Eiswein in Germany and Austria, is made from grapes left on the vine until they freeze, at minus 7 degrees Celsius or colder. They are picked and pressed while frozen. The water stays as ice, so only drops of very sweet, acidic juice flow. Canada's Niagara Peninsula and Okanagan, and Germany, are the main producers.
Ice wine: picked frozen, at minus 7 or colder
For true ice wine, grapes must freeze naturally on the vine.
Yes. In Canada, Germany and Austria, the law requires natural freezing. Freezing grapes artificially, called cryoextraction, cannot be labelled ice wine there.
Ice wine tastes of pure fruit, like peach and lemon, because it rarely has noble rot. If you taste honey and marmalade, think botrytis instead.
Why is the juice of frozen grapes so sweet?
The water stays frozen, so only concentrated juice flows
Pressing frozen grapes leaves most of the water behind as ice, so the juice that flows is rich in sugar and acid.
Late harvest grapes gain sugar and shrivel on the vine
Ice wine grapes are picked and pressed frozen
Canada, Germany and Austria are the main ice wine producers
Explain how dried grapes can make dry wines

Grapes can be dried after harvest, on straw mats, in lofts or racks, or in the sun. Over weeks or months they lose 30 to 50% of their weight. The method is ancient and found all around the Mediterranean. In Italy it is called appassimento, and the wines are called passito.

Most dried grape wines are sweet: Vin Santo from Tuscany, Recioto della Valpolicella, Sicily's Passito di Pantelleria, and Spain's Pedro Ximénez, dried in the sun. But fermentation can run to dryness too. Amarone della Valpolicella is made from dried Corvina grapes fermented nearly dry, giving a powerful red of around 15 to 16% alcohol.
Amarone is made from dried grapes, but fermented to be nearly ____.
Unlike Recioto, Amarone's fermentation continues until almost all the sugar is gone, giving a powerful, dry red.

Drying doesn't just concentrate sugar. The berries start to oxidise and dry out, adding raisin, fig, dried cherry and chocolate notes. Some grapes get a touch of botrytis in drying lofts too. The result is rich, often high in alcohol, and long-lived.
Match each wine to its region.
Drying grapes is a Mediterranean tradition, from Spain to Sicily.
Drying grapes after picking concentrates sugar, acid and flavour
Vin Santo, Recioto and Pedro Ximénez are sweet dried grape wines
Amarone is made from dried grapes but fermented nearly dry
Explain how sweet wines keep their sugar
Match each method to a wine.
Each method concentrates sugar in a different way.
What stops grey rot from developing instead of noble rot?
Dry afternoons stop the fungus from turning destructive.
Not true. It is made from dried grapes but fermented nearly dry. Recioto is its sweet sibling.
Which grapes are known for great sweet wines thanks to high acidity?
Gewürztraminer can make sweet wines, but its naturally low acidity is a weakness, not a strength.
Ice wine grapes must freeze naturally at minus ____ degrees Celsius or colder.
Minus 7 degrees is the common legal threshold in Canada and Germany.
Sweet wines stop fermentation early or start with concentrated grapes
Noble rot, late harvest, freezing and drying concentrate sugar
High acidity keeps great sweet wines fresh
Amarone shows that dried grapes can also make dry wine
